From the surgery

Sleeping badly is not always a sleep problem

Insomnia is one of the most common complaints in the surgery. Behind it there are often worries, life changes or habits, and the first recommended treatment is not a pill.

By Alejandro Rosàs, family doctor

Few complaints are heard as often in primary care as "I can't sleep". Sometimes insomnia appears after a specific event: a loss, a job change, illness in the family. Other times it sets in gradually, and the person no longer remembers when it began.

Sleep is very sensitive to what happens to us during the day. Worry keeps the brain on alert, and bed becomes the place where, finally in silence, all the rumination appears. Over time, the bed itself becomes associated with being awake and tense: it is learning, in the most psychological sense of the word.

The first-line treatment

Clinical guidelines recommend cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) as the first treatment for chronic insomnia. It includes matching time in bed to actual sleep time, getting up if sleep does not come within a reasonable while, keeping regular hours, reviewing beliefs about sleep ("if I don't sleep eight hours, tomorrow will be a disaster") and learning to manage arousal. Its effects last over time.

Hypnotics can be useful in specific situations and for short periods, but long-term use has known drawbacks: tolerance, dependence, daytime drowsiness and, in older people, a higher risk of falls.

Looking at what lies behind

Asking about sleep often opens the door to other conversations: grief that has not been talked about, anxiety, the exhaustion of caring for someone, drinking alcohol to "switch off". Medical causes such as sleep apnoea or pain also need to be ruled out. Sleeping badly is sometimes the most visible symptom of something that deserves attention.
